summary: Code the existing first-order syntax and proof rules, with finite certificates for enumerable axioms, and prove that checking a proof is primitive recursive.
abstract: Before arithmetic can reason about proofs, a proof must be something that numbers can describe. We encode formulas and finite derivations so that a calculation can check each inference, including substitutions and the conditions on fresh variable names. The checker uses the same first-order proof rules as the earlier calculus. When a theory’s axioms can be listed by a program, a proof carries finite evidence that each assumption appears in that enumeration. Checking this evidence never requires waiting indefinitely. The resulting primitive-recursive test accepts exactly the certified proofs, so provability becomes the existence of a numerical certificate.
